cards.title: Private supplier vs. AliExpress: understand the middleman model
cards.summary: A private supplier is a middleman who sources from Chinese factories/1688, routes goods through their own warehouse, then ships to your customer with better speed and pricing than public marketplaces.
cards.use_when: Deciding which fulfillment route to use for a dropshipping store, or explaining supply-chain options before sourcing a product
steps: Define the chain: your supplier's agent buys from a network of Chinese warehouses (including 1688, described as the Chinese equivalent of Alibaba/AliExpress), receives goods at their own warehouse in about 2-3 days, then dispatches to your customer.

Note that most Chinese warehouses are 'general' (hundreds of products) while some are niche-specific (toys, supplements, clothing) — a good supplier knows which warehouse makes the best version of a given product.
Expect the supplier to negotiate both price and shipping line on your behalf, since they do not manufacture — their value is warehouse network access and negotiation.

Compare against AliExpress/Alibaba: typically 10-15 day delivery, limited or no branding, and (per the source) weaker customer support; AliExpress faster options exist but at much higher product cost.
Treat this as a working relationship: suppliers lower your quoted cost as they see consistent daily order volume.
caveats: This is a dropshipping-specific supply model; if you hold inventory or manufacture, the tradeoffs differ.
Supplier quality varies — the source warns a bad supplier means poor product quality, refunds and chargebacks.
Warehouse counts, delivery-day ranges and marketplace speed claims are the source's general figures, not guarantees for a specific supplier.

cards.title: Request the right shipping line to balance cost and speed
cards.summary: Choose a premium shipping line that keeps delivery inside roughly 6-10 days without overpaying, because slow delivery drives chargebacks.
cards.use_when: Configuring fulfillment with a private supplier or 3PL, or evaluating whether a quoted shipping cost is acceptable
steps: Ask your supplier for a premium fast line rather than the default; the source names Uni Express as its preferred line for the best cost-to-speed balance after testing many lines.

Use the supplier's product view to compare lines: for one US-bound product the default line showed 8-15 days, while switching to the faster line (named 'Yune' in the demo, likely the same family) gave 5-8 day shipping for about $3 more per unit added to COGS.

Judge the upgrade against your economics: the source argues roughly 8-15 days (about a week to a week and a half) is acceptable for beginners, and 5-8 days is 'a little overkill' unless margins or AOV/bundling can absorb the extra $3.
Check destination sensitivity: the same product shipping to the UK was notably cheaper and faster than to the US — US from China is typically the most expensive route.
Note that China has 10+ shipping lines with a general pattern: slower lines (10-15 days) cost less, faster lines (6-10 days) cost more.
caveats: Line names and per-unit surcharges are illustrative examples from the source and will change — re-quote before committing.
The source's opinion is that 14-day delivery is no longer acceptable to customers; treat it as the presenter's positioning, not an industry rule.
The $3 upgrade math only works if your AOV or bundle price supports it.
cards.source_name: The Best Supplier For Branded Dropshipping in 2026 (It's Free!).docx

cards.title: Get the product quote low enough that retail pricing stays viable
cards.summary: COGS is a primary lever on net margin — negotiate supplier quotes down and track how small per-unit savings compound across order volume.
cards.use_when: Quoting a product with a supplier, setting retail price, or reviewing net margin after a test
steps: Separate the two components you actually pay: product cost plus shipping to the customer. Nothing else is owed under a free fulfillment platform.
Get an initial quote as a new seller: the source's wallet example was about $7 per unit with no order history — realistic for a beginner, not a blocker.
Ask again once you are moving volume: the same wallet can drop to about $5.50. The $1.50 difference is about $5,000 extra profit across 1,000 orders.
Check whether your supplier lowers the price automatically as order volume grows; the source says a good one will, but you should still ask periodically.
Sanity-check the retail implication: high COGS forces a higher customer price and reduces purchase conversion, so a cheap quote makes profitable ad spend easier to achieve.
Keep net margin (what you actually take home after ads and COGS) as the headline metric rather than revenue.
caveats: The $7/$5.50/$1.50 numbers are the source's illustration, not a benchmark you can assume.
The source attributes its own high-margin screenshots to its private supplier; those income figures are promotional and should not be treated as expected results.
Volume tiers and negotiation leverage depend on the individual supplier.

cards.title: Add branded packaging once a product is proven
cards.summary: Custom logos, mailers and thank-you inserts turn a commodity dropship item into a defensible brand and reduce undercutting.
cards.use_when: A product has validated sales and you want to protect margin from copycat competitors
steps: Wait until the product is proven profitable before spending on branding — the source stresses this is a post-validation upgrade, not a launch step.
Instruct the supplier to add a custom logo on the product, branded mailer packaging and an internal thank-you card.
Use the fulfillment platform's packaging section to select mailer type and then connect that packaging to the specific product, so all future orders use it automatically.
Treat the goal as building a real brand rather than repeatedly flipping and restarting stores every few months.
Expect branding to make it harder for generic competitors to undercut your exact offer, since they cannot replicate the unboxing experience.
caveats: Branding adds cost and complexity per order; the source explicitly ties it to validated demand.
Custom packaging cannot be done through plain AliExpress/Alibaba marketplace orders according to the source, so it requires a private supplier or agent.

cards.title: Add your fulfillment app as a Shopify location or checkout breaks
cards.summary: After installing a 3PL app you must manually register it as a Shopify fulfillment location, otherwise the storefront shows out-of-stock or add-to-cart failures.
cards.use_when: Setting up a new fulfillment/3PL integration on Shopify
steps: Sign up for the fulfillment platform using the same email as your Shopify account, then click 'add store' / 'authorize store' and follow the prompts to install the app on your Shopify dashboard.
After authorizing, open Shopify Settings → Shipping and Delivery.
Click the fulfillment locations icon and add the fulfillment app explicitly as a location (e.g. add 'Team Drop'), then save.
Confirm the app can both see your products/orders and act as a recognized fulfillment location — the app connection alone is not sufficient.
Troubleshoot by symptom: if a product shows 'out of stock' or customers cannot add to cart, the missing fulfillment location is the likely cause.
Note the fulfilment app is free with no monthly fee (contrasted with AutoDS and Zendrop subscriptions), so you only pay COGS.
Verify the current Shopify and app interface steps yourself — menu names and app screens change over time.
caveats: Exact Shopify menu naming and app screens may differ from the source's walkthrough; verify before relying on it.
Pricing and 'free' claims about any platform should be re-checked at signup.
cards.source_name: The Best Supplier For Branded Dropshipping in 2026 (It's Free!).docx

cards.title: Pre-fund a 3PL wallet so orders fulfill automatically
cards.summary: Fulfillment networks debit a pre-funded balance as Shopify orders arrive, removing manual order entry; top up by bank transfer/wire.
cards.use_when: Automating order fulfillment after connecting a private supplier or 3PL to Shopify
steps: Understand the model: orders sync from Shopify automatically, and the platform debits your wallet for product + shipping as each order comes in.
Open the platform's top-up/billing section, choose an amount, and submit.
Fund via the provided bank transfer/wire details (the source calls wire the easiest option); platform-received funds then cover COGS.
Expect payment processing to occur within roughly 24 hours and orders to move from 'awaiting payment' to 'awaiting collection' once purchased from the source warehouse.

Track order states in the orders/purchase-order dashboard: awaiting payment, awaiting collection (order placed with warehouse, in transit to supplier's warehouse), shipped, delivered, completed, and a separate canceled tab.
Keep the balance topped up — a low balance stalls fulfillment and creates delays.
caveats: Bank/wire top-ups can add friction and transfer time; plan for a buffer balance before scaling ad spend.
Processing-time and status-label details are platform-specific and may change.

cards.title: Source products through an agent on WhatsApp
cards.summary: A dedicated agent can source a product from a photo or marketplace link and return a quote, giving beginners support that public marketplaces lack.
cards.use_when: You have identified a product to sell but need a supplier quote, or you need help resolving a fulfillment issue
steps: Contact the assigned agent via the platform's WhatsApp button (the source says every signup gets a dedicated agent at no extra cost).
Send a picture of the product; if you have an AliExpress or Alibaba link, include it to speed up the search.

Wait for the quote and confirm the shipping line, then list the product on your Shopify store — either through the platform's 'list to store' flow or by creating it directly in Shopify and linking it.
If listing inside the platform, choose your store ID, enter product info and images; you can edit the listing in Shopify afterward and the link stays intact.
Use the agent for post-purchase problems too, e.g. 'tracking says delivered but the customer can't find it' — a supplier can trace it and send a replacement unit.
Consider buying a sample first; the source highlights sample purchase as an option it had not seen on competing platforms.
caveats: Agent quality varies, and the source frames supplier support as a key differentiator of private suppliers versus raw marketplaces.
Response speed from an agent is not guaranteed.
cards.source_name: The Best Supplier For Branded Dropshipping in 2026 (It's Free!).docx

cards.title: Why the source rejects subscription fulfillment platforms and raw marketplaces
cards.summary: The presenter argues AliExpress/Alibaba and paid tools like AutoDS/Zendrop are poor options vs. a free private-supplier platform, on grounds of speed, branding, support and monthly fees.
cards.use_when: Choosing between marketplace dropshipping, paid fulfillment SaaS, and a private supplier/agent
steps: Evaluate marketplaces on four axes the source calls out: shipping time (10-15 days typical), ability to brand, cost of faster options (a wallet example jumped to ~$40 for an 8-day AliExpress shipment), and customer support.

Evaluate paid platforms on the subscription question: the source argues it should not cost a monthly fee to have orders fulfilled and shipped, and dislikes paying for sourcing on top of a subscription.

Weigh the source's counter-position that a free private-supplier platform plus agent is more beginner-friendly, since beginners may not have a validated product yet and extra fees compound risk early.
Check that a candidate free platform provides the features you need before switching: supplier network, shipping-line choice, branding options, agent/WhatsApp support, and profile/store integration.
Verify the current fee structure and features directly with each provider — pricing and terms change.
caveats: This is a presenter's opinion delivered while promoting one platform; treat the 'never use these' framing as positioning, not neutral advice.
Competing platforms (AutoDS, Zendrop) offer features not discussed here — evaluate against your own needs.
The source receives signup bonuses/coupons for its recommended platform, so its comparison is not disinterested.

cards.title: Judge net margin and refunds as the real supply-chain KPI
cards.summary: Low COGS plus reliable, traceable delivery protects net margin and prevents revenue loss to refunds and chargebacks.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether a supplier or shipping line is worth keeping
steps: Track net margin — the share of revenue you actually keep — with ads and COGS as the two biggest expense lines the source names.
Treat product quality as a supply-chain variable, since multiple warehouses make the same item and a bad pick causes refunds and chargebacks.
Recognize the escalation the source warns about: enough chargebacks can lead to withheld payments or loss of the Shopify account.
Give customers tracking numbers so they can follow delivery — the source treats this as part of the standard service level, not a nice-to-have.
Use delivery speed as a chargeback-reduction tool: 6-10 days was cited as the target window, with roughly a week being acceptable.
Re-quote and re-check the supplier relationship periodically rather than assuming the initial terms hold.
caveats: Chargeback and account-closure outcomes depend on processor and platform policies; the source states them as a risk, not a certainty.
The source's own margin screenshots are promotional and are not evidence of typical results.
